name: onnxruntime

facts.description: ONNX Runtime: cross-platform, high performance ML inferencing and training accelerator

title: ONNX Runtime: Cross-Platform Inference and Training Engine for AI Models
answer: ONNX Runtime is Microsoft's open source engine for running and training machine learning models in the ONNX format, written in C++ under the MIT licence. It sits between your trained model and the hardware, using execution providers to accelerate inference on CPUs, GPUs, NPUs and browsers. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its biggest wins come from model conversion and quantization, so you should expect an optimization step before deployment rather than dropping in an unmodified model.

sections.body: ONNX Runtime is made by Microsoft and lives in the microsoft/onnxruntime repository on GitHub, where it has gathered around 22,000 stars. It is a cross-platform, high performance machine learning inferencing and training accelerator, written in C++ and released under the MIT licence, with its official home at onnxruntime.ai. It first appeared in the years before the 1.5.2 release, since the ORT model format documentation notes support from version 1.5.2 onward, and the site describes releases through 1.17 and beyond. In the AI stack it occupies the runtime layer, the piece that takes a model already trained elsewhere and executes it efficiently on whatever hardware is available, rather than the layer where models are defined or trained from scratch. It is closely tied to the ONNX model format, an open and portable representation, and it is the engine that turns that format into running predictions.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs are inference first and training second. On the inference side the site documents acceleration of over 130,000 open source models from Hugging Face, generative work with Phi-2, Mistral, CodeLlama and Orca-2, image generation with SD Turbo and SDXL Turbo through Olive, and browser inference through WebGPU and WebAssembly. It is strongest where a model must run across many platforms with hardware-specific acceleration, which is why Goodnotes used it to ship a scribble-to-erase feature on Windows, Web and Android from one in-house LSTM model, and why it appears in mobile, web, embedded Linux and data centre deployments. Training is supported through the torch-ort package and the ORTModule API, part of the PyTorch ecosystem and the Azure Container for PyTorch, with the same model and APIs working on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. It is also used for data-adjacent optimization work through Olive, which handles quantization and fine-tuning decisions. Where it is the best choice is on-device and cross-platform deployment, especially when latency, memory and offline operation matter.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The learning curve is moderate and mostly practical rather than mathematical. A developer needs comfort with Python for the conversion and optimization tooling, some familiarity with a training framework such as PyTorch or TensorFlow to produce the original model, and a working understanding of model formats, quantization and hardware targets to make good use of execution providers. Systems knowledge helps when choosing between CPU, GPU and NPU paths, and when reasoning about compilation and caching, since the Vitis AI provider compiles a model when the session starts and that compilation can take minutes before the first inference. The official site offers substantial documentation, including execution provider pages, model optimization guides and a blog with worked examples, which is enough for a beginner to follow along, though the material assumes you already have a model and a deployment target in mind.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem is broad and mostly documented on the official site. Execution providers cover CPU through WSAM, GPUs and NPUs through WebNN and WebGPU, NVIDIA through CUDA and TensorRT, and AMD through Vitis AI for Ryzen AI, Adaptable SoCs and Alveo cards. Olive serves as the model optimization toolkit, with quantization algorithms including AWQ and GPTQ, and a shared cache backed by Azure Storage for team collaboration. The torch-ort package connects training to PyTorch, and ORT training is composable with DeepSpeed and Megatron. Documentation covers the ORT format for size-constrained builds, conversion scripts, and per-provider installation and configuration. Community support is visible through the repository, the blog and the integrations with Hugging Face models, though the facts here do not quantify forum or chat activity.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: It is built for both, but the emphasis is production performance and memory control. Prototyping is straightforward because ONNX is a portable format and the Goodnotes team reported simple integration during their prototype, and because a full build accepts ordinary ONNX models without conversion. Production is where the tuning lives, through execution providers, float16 and int4 quantization, the ORT format for reduced size builds on mobile and web, and choices such as Fixed versus Runtime optimization style depending on whether a compiling provider like NNAPI or CoreML is in play. The cost is an extra optimization and conversion step, a build configuration file in some workflows, and provider-specific setup such as installing Ryzen AI Software for AMD targets. The payoff is documented speed, including up to 20.48x improvement over PyTorch with int4 quantization for Phi-2 and large browser speedups with WebGPU.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: Adoption is real and current rather than legacy. Microsoft maintains it, it is part of the PyTorch ecosystem through torch-ort and the Azure Container for PyTorch, and it is used by product teams such as Goodnotes for a cross-platform AI feature. The site describes acceleration of over 130,000 Hugging Face models and integrations with AMD, Arm KleidiAI, NVIDIA TensorRT and browser standards, which places it among the standard runtimes for deployment rather than a niche tool. For someone choosing what to learn, that means skills in ONNX Runtime transfer to on-device, edge, browser and data centre deployment work, and they pair naturally with PyTorch training experience. The facts here do not include salary data or job counts, so any claim about specific career outcomes would go beyond what the site supports.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: ONNX Runtime is typically used with Python for conversion, optimization and scripting, and with C++ or C# when embedding the runtime in an application, since the engine itself is written in C++. It sits beside training frameworks rather than replacing them, taking models exported from PyTorch or TensorFlow, and it works with optimization tools such as Olive, quantizers from AMD and Vitis AI, and acceleration libraries like DeepSpeed and Megatron for training. The polyglot pattern is a training framework in Python producing an ONNX model, an optimization pass that may quantize or convert to ORT format, and then a runtime embedded in a native or web application, with execution providers selecting the hardware underneath. That division of labour is the point, each language and tool doing the part it is best at.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site is candid about some weaknesses. Quantization can affect model quality, though the Olive blog found the impact small as measured by perplexity, and int4 quantization typically performs best at batch size 1 because of a special GemV kernel. Compilation for providers like Vitis AI can take minutes before the first inference, which is awkward for interactive development. Some integrations are experimental, such as Olive support in the Vitis AI provider, and supported arguments and defaults differ across versions, so scripts are not always portable between releases. The official material does not say how large the community is, how frequently releases ship beyond the versions mentioned, or how ONNX Runtime compares on cost and energy use, and it does not settle which provider is best for a given model without benchmarking.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
